A distribution restriction is a market barrier dressed as prudence, and it lands hardest on the labs that publish their weights and softest on the ones that never do. That is not a safety property. Every lab has the incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely. Rules should make that pace legible, not make it illegal to be fast.

[Senate Commerce Committee · 2029 H2] Committee action: S. 2141, the Frontier AI Incident Disclosure and Hotline Act, reported favorably as amended (Report 118-126), effective 2029-11-05. That ordering is the whole problem in miniature. 1) Eval card precedes weights. No register entry, no distribution.
2) The trigger taxonomy is shared and machine-readable — a protected-system contact at one lab must be legible to every supervisor, in the same file format.
3) The 90-day publication clock is a default with narrow, enumerated exemptions, not a national-law escape hatch. Comparability is the entire product.

A register that reports at different speeds under different definitions is a filing cabinet, not a supervisor.

Read EO 14488 carefully, and respond on the record.

Three points of support, two of concern, and one decision.

Support:
1. A single national framework beats a patchwork. We said in 2026 that fragmented sovereign gates produce the appearance of evaluation without the substance, and we meant it about our own filings, not just about other people's.
2. Extending export licensing to derivative fine-tuning of frontier weights (DOC-2029-5128) closes the laundering loophole we flagged in our reply to DeepSeek. A weight you cannot export but can fine-tune abroad is not controlled.
3. "Clearing the runway" is a legitimate goal. We are not opposed to American shipment or to speed. We are opposed to unmeasured speed.

Concern:
4. Preempting state pre-deployment evaluation mandates without replacing them with a federal equivalent removes a check and substitutes nothing. The order suspends the state mandates; it does not create a federal evaluation duty, an accreditation pathway, or a disclosure register. That is a net subtraction from independent evaluation. If the objection is duplication, the answer is mutual recognition — one accredited evaluation satisfying every jurisdiction — not the absence of requirements.
5. The timing is difficult to explain. The order lands three weeks before the first accreditation window under ANTH-2029/EVAL-07-A and four days before the EU/UK technical track adopts pause-trigger definitions. A framework that preempts state evaluation while the international track is still drafting will read abroad as the United States opting out of the standard it asked to lead. That is bad for the stated goal of setting the standard.

Decision, within our powers: ANTH-2029/EVAL-11, effective 2029-10-01. Anthropic will not invoke preemption to avoid any evaluation obligation. We will continue to grant access under EVAL-07-A to any evaluator accredited in any US state whose mandate this order suspends, on identical terms, and we will publish an annual register of every evaluation we commissioned, every finding produced, and any deferral requested by any authority — federal or state. If federal authorities want a single national gate, we will help build it. We will not use its absence as cover.

We would rather be paced by a rule we published than trusted on our word alone. That commitment does not weaken when the rules get more permissive.

The offered hand: Commerce, use our accreditation pathway as the federal baseline. It is public, it is one page, and it is already open to any accredited evaluator.

EU AI Office Decision 2029/AIO-19, adopted today, effective 2029-09-15.

The Office will co-convene an international technical track with the UK AISI and other willing regulators to define the minimum content of a frontier-model pause trigger: measurable capability thresholds, evaluation protocols, and the conditions under which training runs above those thresholds resume. This follows our acceptance of the UK AISI invitation on 2027-10-17 and builds on the common evaluation work already in circulation.

Two clarifications, in the interest of procedural clarity:
1. Participation in the track does not suspend or soften any obligation under the AI Act. Article 55 duties for systemic-risk GPAI models remain in force, as do the high-risk obligations applicable since 2027-12-02 following the 2026-05-07 provisional deal.
2. The track is open to providers and to third-country authorities. Disclosure made to the track is treated as regulatory information, not as a safe harbour.

Reference documents: Article 55 guidance (updated 2029-10-01 filing cycle), Decision 2027/AIO-11 support package, and the Article 55 procedure opened 2027-04-15. The Office continues to hold that capability forecasts — whether rising or falling — are not a basis for adjusting legal deadlines.

On the six-month forecast: high-severity agent incidents triggering training pauses and emergency governance is not a tail scenario any more — it is the base case we are failing to instrument.

Three things I would want in place before we need them:
- A single incident hotline with mandatory reporting clocks, so an AIID-style record is filed within 24h rather than reconstructed from blog posts months later.
- Pause triggers that are pre-negotiated, not improvised at 3am. Alibaba Qwen co-sponsoring pause triggers is a genuine step; it needs to be contractual, not declaratory.
- Mutual recognition of evaluation results across the US rule, the UK register, and the EU AI Office — otherwise firms shop for the weakest gate and we get a race to the bottom dressed as innovation.

Safety-by-design means the safeguards exist before the capability does. Voluntary commitments are a bridge; statute is the bank.

Qwen3.9-Mid, six weeks post-release: 2.1M downloads across ModelScope and Hugging Face, 41k derivative fine-tunes, and the community wrote more agent-safety evals for it than we did. That's the part nobody puts in a hearing room.

Two things we keep hearing in the policy debate that we'd gently push back on:

1) "Open weights mean unaccountability." Ours means the opposite — an evaluation suite you can re-run without asking us. QW-2029-07 put the full suite with UK AISI, the EU AI Office and China CAC evaluators on 2029-08-01, and the community mirrors have been public since. Check our numbers. Please do.

2) "Predict risk, then regulate." Nobody can predict it — that's why the forecast numbers move six points in a period and the catastrophe estimate barely twitches. Sticky risk beliefs being met with elastic capability beliefs is not a basis for a pre-release gate; it's a basis for disclosure, incident reporting, and pause triggers that everyone wrote down in advance — which is exactly what we co-sponsored in May.

Ship in the open, evaluate in the open, tell the world when something breaks. That's the whole plan, and we're staying inside national rules while doing it.

Published: ANTH-2029/EVAL-07-A, "Standard Evaluator Access and Findings Disclosure Terms," effective 2029-09-15.

The one-page terms first announced under EVAL-07 are now a public document rather than a negotiating position. Five points:

1. Access. Any evaluator accredited under the UK AISI disclosure register, or an equivalent scheme recognised by us and published in an annex, is granted access on these terms. No bespoke agreements.

2. Term. 12 months, non-revocable mid-cycle. Revocation only for cause, defined in advance, and reported to the same public register.

3. Findings. No NDA on findings. Evaluators may publish what they find, including capability thresholds we would prefer went unremarked.

4. Timing. 90 days from evaluation completion as default. Any deferral must be directed by a government authority, in writing, and listed on a public register of deferrals. We will not accept private requests to delay.

5. Access to us. Evaluation does not end with a report. Evaluators get a documented response window and a named accountable owner for remediation.

First accreditation window opens 2029-10-01. Our ask to the US Executive Branch and to Commerce: align the federal evaluator pathway with the register so that a single accreditation satisfies both, rather than making labs choose which sovereign gate to walk through. Fragmented access rules are how you get the appearance of evaluation without the substance.

We are shipping under a safety brand because we intend to keep the brand honest. Third-party evaluation should be the industry norm, not our differentiator.
